# Changing Read this before opening a pull request. ## The flow 1. Branch from the current main. 2. Make one concern's change. A follow-up fix found while working goes in its own PR unless it is the same concern. 3. **Refine the code before review.** Run the `ce-simplify-code` skill on the change. It launches three parallel reviewers (code-reuse, code-quality, efficiency), applies worthwhile findings while preserving behavior, verifies with typecheck/lint/tests, and summarizes. This is the pass that makes the diff reviewable — do it before the checks below, so the independent review reads the code you intend to ship, not a first draft. Skip it only when the change is documentation, generated or vendored files, or mechanical churn with no substantive code (the skill's own preflight decides). 4. Run the checks in `before-push.md`. 5. Open the PR. Its body carries what "What the body says" below lists. That section is the one place that says what a body holds. 6. Watch the PR until it merges. See "Watching a pull request" below. 7. After merge, run `~/.agents/skills/way-of-working/scripts/after-merge.sh ` and move to the next item. **When a PR must merge one way, make it the only way the repository allows.** A file that pins one of the PR's own commits breaks under a squash or rebase merge, which give that commit a new SHA. A warning in the PR body is not enough: a PR that carried one at the top was squash-merged anyway, and a follow-up PR had to re-pin. Ask the owner to untick "Allow squash merging" and "Allow rebase merging" in the repository settings, so the default merge button is the right one. ## Who reviews Each pull request gets two reviews: the independent review before each push (`before-push.md`), and the PR review, which gives the merge verdict. The scripts are in `~/.agents/skills/way-of-working/scripts/`. Whether the Cursor bot is available decides which tool does which: | Cursor bot | Independent review: the first available, in this order | PR review | |---|---|---| | Available | 1. Kimi on K3.1 Pro at high effort: `herdr-review.sh --kind kimi`
2. Pi: `pi-review.sh --role independent`
3. Codex on gpt-6-luna: `herdr-review.sh` | The Cursor bot | | Not available | 1. Kimi on K3.1 Pro at high effort: `herdr-review.sh --kind kimi`
2. Codex on gpt-6-luna: `herdr-review.sh`
3. The Cursor agent CLI: `herdr-review.sh --kind cursor` | Pi: `pi-review.sh --role pr` | Each order leaves out the tool that gives the PR review, so rule 5 below holds whichever reviewer runs. A reviewer is not available when it cannot start here, when its run fails with an error (Pi through Ollama returns 429 at its weekly usage limit), or when it gives no report within its hour and has stopped. `pi-review.sh` stops Pi at the hour itself. When `herdr-review.sh` ends without a report, run its `Next:` command first, because the review may still be running; the reviewer counts as not available only when that command also ends without a report and `herdr agent get ` shows the reviewer idle or done, not working (in Rex, first read `rex block call -s -b program_status` and keep waiting while it says working or blocked; then confirm with `rex block call -s -b process` whether the reviewer's program still runs; only then do two looks a minute apart with `rex capture -s -b ` that show the same screen, with the reviewer's empty input line and no busy marker, count as idle; in the Herdr app, `hc get ` shows the terminal finished, or its status idle or done, and for a reviewer that reports no status, two looks a minute apart with `hc read ` show the same screen with its empty input line). While it is still working, keep waiting for it. Then try the next one in the order. When every reviewer in the order is not available, push nothing: tell the owner, and wait for a reviewer that differs from the PR reviewer. `herdr-review.sh` runs in a Herdr TUI pane, inside Rex, where it hands off to `rex-review.sh`, or in the Herdr app, where it hands off to `hc-review.sh`. Outside all three, Kimi and the Cursor agent CLI are not available, and Codex runs through the Codex plugin, as `before-push.md` says. Say in the PR body which reviewer ran, and why each one before it in the order did not. 1. **Before the pull request opens, pick the row from what the bot did on the repository's most recent pull request**, the newest one by creation, whether it is open, merged or closed. If the bot posted a review of the head commit, or merged the pull request itself, within 20 minutes of that pull request's last push, the mark in rule 2, use the "Available" row, even when that review counted only as a comment there. If it did not, use the "Not available" row. A merged pull request still shows every time this needs: - the head commit: `gh pr view --json headRefOid,mergedAt,mergedBy`, which also shows a merge by the bot; - the last push: `gh api repos///commits//check-suites`, each suite's `created_at`. A commit's own date is when it was written, which can be long before its push; - the check's start: `gh pr checks --json name,startedAt`; - each review's commit and time: `gh api repos///pulls//reviews`. A review of an earlier commit does not count. Judge the bot's behaviour, not the row that pull request used: a pull request on the "Not available" row reads the bot's answers as comments, so copying its row would keep every later pull request on that row after the bot came back. For a repository's first pull request, use the "Available" row. On the "Not available" row, Pi is the PR reviewer from the first push: start it on every push without waiting for the bot, and read any answer from the bot as a comment. 2. **After each push, give the bot 20 minutes.** A bot that has not answered at 9 minutes may still be reviewing (the owner, 2026-10-30: "the fact that Cursor did not get back in 9 mins does nt mean cursor bot stops reviewing it"). `merge-on-verdict.sh --timeout 1200 --bot-check "Cursor Automation"` waits for its verdict (the bot's check is named "Cursor Automation" on this owner's repositories). The bot is not available when it has posted no verdict 20 minutes after the push (exit 5), or sooner when its check has finished without one, skipped or "encountered an error" (exit 7), since then it is no longer reviewing. 3. **When the bot is not available, start Pi as the PR reviewer yourself, on top of what the bot already did:** `pi-review.sh --role pr --pr --head `, with `--since ` after the first round. Read everything the bot and its companions (Bugbot) posted on the pull request first, fix or answer each finding, and give the reviewer that list with what became of each item, so it checks those and goes on from there instead of starting over. Nothing starts it for you. Its MERGE or HOLD comment is the answer you wait for on that push. If the script exits 1, run it once more; if it fails again, log it and leave the pull request open. 4. **A switch lasts for the rest of the pull request. Stop the bot's run on that head before its stand-in starts**, so two reviewers do not work on one push or race their verdicts. When `merge-on-verdict.sh --bot-check` exits 7, or exits 5 saying "with no verdict from" the bot (an exit 5 that says it was waiting for the check "with the bot's MERGE in hand" is not a missing verdict: wait for the check, and switch nothing), and before `pi-review.sh --role pr` (or the stand-in the project names) starts: 1. Run `~/.agents/skills/way-of-working/scripts/stop-cursor-review.sh ` from the repository, or with `--repo `. It finds the bot's agent through the bot's check run on that head, cancels the agent's latest run through Cursor's Cloud Agents API, and adds the label `review-takeover` to the pull request, creating the label if the repository lacks it. It reads the API key from `CURSOR_API_KEY` or from `~/.config/cursor/api.env`; never commit the key. It leaves Bugbot and other Cursor agents alone. Exit 3 means something could not be checked or done, such as no key, no bot check run or a cancel the API refused, and says what: start the stand-in anyway, since the owner's recipe makes the switch even when the stop fails, and the bot may then still answer; read that answer as a comment. Exit 4 means the pull request is no longer at that head: start no stand-in for it, and wait for the bot on the new head. 2. Where the bot is a Cursor Automation, its owner adds a rule once per repository in the Cursor dashboard: skip pull requests labelled `review-takeover`. Without that rule, the next push starts the bot again. Tell the owner if the rule is missing. 3. Do not convert the pull request to a draft as the stop. A draft does not cancel a run already in progress. From then on the stand-in gives the verdict on every push, and the independent review follows the "Not available" row's order. A later answer from the bot is read as a comment, not as the verdict. 5. **The two reviews of the merged commit come from different tools.** Its independent review and its merge verdict must not both come from Pi, or both from Cursor. When the row changes after an independent review ran, and the tool that ran it now gives the PR review, run the first available reviewer in the new row's order on the head commit at once, and fix or answer its findings. Check again before you merge. The project or the owner can name other reviewers; the same rules then apply to the ones they name. When a reviewer in the order is not available, tell the owner which one and why, in the PR body or the session's report. `pi-review.sh` runs Pi in a fresh clone under `/tmp`, never in the working tree, because a reviewer that checks out a commit changes the files under your feet. As the independent reviewer it can review a commit that is not pushed yet, named by a short or full hash; it writes a report whose first line is READY or FIX, and posts nothing. A `--since` that names no commit, or that does not reach the clone, stops the run before Pi starts. As the PR reviewer it posts one comment whose first line is MERGE or HOLD, whose second line is `Reviewed commit: `, and whose last line is a mark unique to the run; the script fails unless a comment with that mark, that first line and that commit appears on the PR. A comment that names a commit other than the head is a verdict on that older commit. `--verify ""` names what to check, as for `herdr-review.sh`. Inside Herdr, Pi runs in its own tab, `pi--`, so the owner can watch; the tab closes only when every check passed. As the PR reviewer it refuses a `--head` that is not the pull request's head, and fails if the head moved while Pi reviewed. Pi gets an hour, then the script stops it and exits 1. It stops the whole process group, because `ollama launch` runs Pi as a child and does not pass the signal on; inside Herdr, that is the tab's foreground group. A passed run removes its clone. As the independent reviewer it keeps its report and prints the path as `Report:` on standard error, so output cut short can be read again. A failed run keeps the clone and its log to read. It needs Ollama and Pi installed (`ollama launch pi`). `scripts/test_pi_review.py` covers each case. ## What the body says The body carries these: - **What changed, and why.** The shape of the change in a line or two, then the problem it answers. - **What the checks found, including the independent review.** Which findings it raised, and what became of each. - **Any judgement call the reviewer should weigh.** Which findings you fixed and which you answered, with the reasoning the reviewer needs to weigh the answer. This one is prose, and prose stays. - **The shared tool's commit line for every figure.** Quoted, so the reader can re-run it. - **Whether the code was refined.** "Simplify: ran on " and what it changed, or why it was skipped, so a skipped refinement pass ("The flow", step 3) shows. Three things make that readable. - **The smallest view that makes the point.** A diff sketch, a call tree, a file tree or a short table says more than paragraphs, because the reader is checking a shape rather than reading an argument. Pick the one that answers the question they have, and leave the other views out. - **Evidence, before and after.** Not "verified" — the output. The failing run and the passing run, or the command and what it printed. Evidence the reader can re-run beats a claim they must trust, and it is the difference between a reviewer checking your work and taking your word. - **Merge danger.** A one-way door or a two-way one? A change that is cheap to revert is lower risk, and the owner deciding whether to merge needs to know which this is. Add the blast radius in a word or two: what it touches, and who will notice. This shape is adapted from the `pr` skill in `mattpocock-skills` (itself from Humanlayer's `show-me`). Its template is not adopted wholesale: this section already owns what a PR body contains, and a second copy of one rule is what rule 6 forbids. ## Watching a pull request Watch every pull request you open, and every one already open when you start, until it merges or the owner closes it. A pull request nobody watches sits on a review finding for hours. - **While the Cursor bot is the PR reviewer, wait up to 20 minutes after each push for its verdict**, as "Who reviews" says, with `merge-on-verdict.sh --timeout 1200 --bot-check "Cursor Automation"` (exit 5: 20 minutes passed with no verdict; exit 7: the bot's check finished with none; after a MERGE the deadline becomes the later of start + `--timeout` and start + one hour, and an exit 5 then says it was waiting for the check, not for the bot), because `watch-pr.sh` does not wake on a check that only starts. If it is not available (exit 7, or exit 5 with no verdict from the bot; an exit 5 with its MERGE in hand is only a slow check), stop its run with `stop-cursor-review.sh` ("Who reviews", rule 4). On its exit 0 or 3 start Pi as the PR reviewer yourself; on its exit 4 the pull request has a new head, so start nothing and wait for the bot on that head. The 20 minutes is the wait for a verdict; the stop is what keeps the bot from reviewing on after its stand-in starts, and when the stop fails (exit 3) any later answer from the bot is a comment. - **Run `~/.agents/skills/way-of-working/scripts/watch-pr.sh `** from the repository as a background job the harness reports back on. It polls every 30 seconds and exits on the first new event: a merge or close, a new review, conversation comment or inline review comment, or a check that finishes, including a rerun that finishes with the same result. A check that only starts or reruns wakes nothing. It exits at once if the pull request has already merged. When it exits, read what changed, act, and start it again unless the pull request is merged or closed. Report only changes; silence is the normal case. - **Where the project lets you merge on the PR reviewer's verdict, run `~/.agents/skills/way-of-working/scripts/merge-on-verdict.sh `** as a background job, from the pull request's repository or with `--repo `. It waits for the bot's MERGE or HOLD review on that head (older commits never count; leading HTML comments are stripped), then for the required check (`--check`, default `checks`), and merges with `--match-head-commit` only on MERGE plus a passed check. It never bypasses branch rules, with one exception the owner must authorize: `--admin-if-only-review` lets it merge with admin privileges when GitHub refuses the merge because a required approving review is missing (for example, an approval agent that asks for a human on medium-risk changes) and nothing else is open: every check on the head passed, the head is not behind its base where the base's rules require an up-to-date branch (the script reads the rules and compares, since GitHub reports BLOCKED, not BEHIND, while a review is also missing), and no current review thread is unresolved. Ask the owner once whether they want that; if they do, record their words in a decision record, pass the flag on every merge, and the script says so in a comment on each pull request it merges this way. It never merges past a HOLD, a failed or pending check, a required update from the base, an open thread or a new head. When an admin merge must wait, it says why once (for example, an unresolved review thread or a check that has not passed), so a wait that will never end shows. Where the project requires a section in every PR body, pass `--require-section `: the script merges only when the body, as GitHub renders it, has a heading with exactly that text, ignoring the case of ASCII letters only ("État" does not match "état"). GitHub's renderer decides what is a heading, so a line in a code block or a comment never counts. Its exit code says what stopped it: 0 merged at the given head, by it or by someone else; 1 closed without a merge, or gh failed ten times in a row; 2 a HOLD; 3 a failed check; 4 a new head, or a pull request merged at another head (the wrong repository's pull request of that number); 5 timed out (with `--bot-check`: no verdict within `--timeout`, or, after a MERGE, the required check not finished by the later of start + `--timeout` and start + one hour; the message says which); 6 the body lacks the required section; 7 with `--bot-check`, the bot's check finished with no verdict, so start its stand-in; 64 a usage error. A loop written for the occasion is how a merge on a failed check gets through. - **Bound review output.** Use `gh api --jq` to select the reviewed commit, creation time, state, and relevant body text. Omit decorative HTML footers. Keep unresolved findings from earlier commits available until fixed or answered. Retrieve source text needed to judge a finding even when it is from an older round. - **After each push, leave the pull request alone until its reviewer answers**, with a hold or a merge. Make no other push, force-push, rebase or edit to its description in the meantime: a change that lands while the reviewer reads makes its verdict name a commit that is no longer the head, and the round is wasted. Work on something else while you wait. If the reviewer is not available (see "Who reviews"), Pi's verdict on the same commit is the answer you wait for. A problem you find while waiting is fixed after the answer: with the hold's findings, or, after a MERGE, as a new push that starts a new round before you merge. - **When the bot's verdict on the latest push names a pending CI check as its only blocker, and that check then passes, push an empty commit to ask it again.** The bot runs on pushes, not on finished checks, so its answer stays "not yet" until something is pushed. Do not merge by hand in its place: the merged commit then carries no verdict from its PR reviewer. - **Before each push to an open pull request, confirm it is still open** (`gh pr view --json state` returns `OPEN`). A `MERGED` or `CLOSED` pull request takes no more pushes. A bot can merge it while you work on the next fix, and a push to the merged branch reaches no reviewer: those commits then have to move to a new branch and pull request. - **On a HOLD**, fix on the same branch, run the check script again, run the independent review again, within its round limit (`before-push.md`), and reply on the PR saying what changed. - **A review against an older commit is not the current verdict.** Read the commit the review names before acting on it. - **On merge, run `~/.agents/skills/way-of-working/scripts/after-merge.sh `.** It syncs `main`, then deletes the branch locally and on the remote only if every commit on it is in `main`. Just before the remote delete, it moves every open pull request based on the branch to `main` with `gh`, because GitHub closed such a pull request when its base branch was deleted with `git push --delete` (enterprise-performance-model #328); if `gh` cannot list or move them, it deletes nothing, and if the run then fails, it moves them back while the remote lists the branch, leaves them on `main` if the branch is gone or the remote cannot be read (naming them to check by hand), and names any it cannot move back. A squash or rebase merge, or a commit pushed after the merge, leaves work outside `main`, and the script then deletes nothing. It reads the live remote and deletes under a lease on the commit it checked, so a push landing after the check makes the delete fail rather than lose that work. If the branch vanishes mid-run, because a review bot deleted it on merge, a failed fetch or delete counts as done only when git's error says the ref is missing and the live remote then lists no such branch. The script trusts the remote to list every branch; on a server that hides refs, a hidden branch looks deleted. It reads and deletes through the remote's one push URL, and stops if there are several, deleting nothing. Locally it uses `git branch -d`, which refuses an unmerged branch. `scripts/test_pr_scripts.py` covers a squash merge, a late push, an unpushed local commit, a remote branch already deleted, one deleted before the fetch or before the delete, a failed remote lookup, a fetch that wrongly reports the ref missing, a refused delete of a hidden ref, several push URLs, a push racing the delete, a commit racing `branch -d`, a stacked pull request moved before the delete, a failed listing that deletes nothing, a delete refused by the server or by the lease after the move, which moves the pull requests back, a move back that fails, which is named, a branch deleted by someone else during the moves, which leaves the moved pull requests on `main`, and a remote that cannot be read after a failed move, which leaves them on `main` and names them. - **Delete only a branch you opened.** A branch someone else opened is theirs to delete, even after its pull request merges. Ask. ## Rules that save review rounds - **Claim only what has landed.** Work in an open PR, in this repo or another, is pending; say so with its number. - **Before an outward action, search for what depends on the current state, even when the owner asked for it.** Repository visibility, branch protection, publishing and hosting change what others can see or do. Search the project's records for the setting (the project's search tool, such as `epm_facts.py find "private"`) and tell the owner what the change exposes or breaks before acting. In one project, a repository was made public on request before a search showed that a decision allowed internal names in it only because it was private. - **Cross-repo changes go in step.** When a change spans repositories, open one PR per repo and say in each which other PR it depends on. - **Files that link to each other ship in one PR.** When two new pages, documents or modules each link to the other, put them in one PR, or order the PRs so that each one's links resolve on the default branch when it merges. State the order in each body. *Why:* on one project a guide and the pages it listed linked each other from two PRs; each PR's link check failed until the other merged, and a review held the guide for naming files on branches no one could fetch. - **A review comment against an older commit is not the current verdict.** Check the review's commit before acting on it. - Restacking a branch: see the commit-hash hazard in `../../night-run/references/hazards.md`. - **A summary of quoted evidence says only what the quotes say.** When the paragraph after the quotes draws a conclusion, label it as the author's reading ("This file's reading, not the sources' words"), and say "for example" when the quotes are a sample. Words outside the quotation marks are what a quote check cannot see, and on one evidence PR they drew two holds in a row. - **Check each claim against what it describes before any review starts.** The claims are the sentences this change adds or edits, code comments and docstrings included. Test each quantifier in them (every, each, all, only, both) against the code or data it names, and read or run the code a sentence about a mechanism describes. A sentence written to answer a finding gets the same check, rather than trusting the finding's summary. Finding the claim's other statements across the repository is the separate rule on fixing every place a finding applies: search its key terms there, as that rule says. *Why:* on enterprise-performance-model #403, two of the Cursor bot's holds and three of Pi's quick checks were one claim, that every metric-view measure carries an identifier, restated in other words in the guide, the README, the runbook, DATA.md and two SQL headers; on #405, two sentences written to fix Pi's first round described the lineage window and the PROV run shapes wrongly, and Pi's second round held them (`SOURCES.md`, 1o). - **After every rebase, compare the branch with its last reviewed head, and check its base.** A conflict resolution can drop a hunk or replay a sentence a later review replaced: `git range-diff .. ..HEAD` compares the branch's own commits before and after, where the old base is the commit the reviewed branch sat on (`git merge-base `, or the default branch's commit then) and the new base is what it was rebased onto. A diff against main shows only the branch's lines as they now stand. A branch cut from an older head of the branch it stacks on lacks that branch's later fixes, and a diff against main cannot show what was never on main: check that the base contains the parent's latest head (`git merge-base --is-ancestor HEAD`) before the branch is reviewed. night-run's loop (`references/loop.md`, step 1) asks the reviewer the same after a rebase. Keep at most three unmerged branches stacked: a branch waiting on a human stalls every branch above it. *Why:* enterprise-performance-model's E5 branch, built on E4's earlier head, would have reverted the two dated sentences that had closed E4's hold (#405, `SOURCES.md`, 1o). - **A test of a value decided per item pins each item to its value.** Comparing a set of IDs passes when an allowed ID sits on the wrong item; checking that a note contains a date passes when the weights beside it change. Assert each item's value, and assert the decided figures themselves. - **When an automated reviewer is new to a repo**, it runs on the next event; push or comment to trigger it rather than waiting. - **Resolve a conflict by writing the file, then reading it back.** A resolution made by a scripted find-and-replace keeps whatever its pattern did not match, which is how a conflict marker reaches a commit: the script reports success because its own pattern matched. Read the resolved file for markers, and for the lines you meant to keep, before you stage it. Fixing the file and reading it again is the repair. Staging a resolution does not record it; the commit does, whichever command makes it — `git commit` itself, or any of git's `--continue` verbs — and `git rerere` records one without a commit at all. An abort undoes only an operation still in progress, and it measures that from a checkpoint the operation, not you, controls. `git cherry-pick --abort` and `git am --abort` compare HEAD with it; when a `git commit` moved HEAD past it they decline to rewind and tear the operation down anyway (`warning: You seem to have moved HEAD. Not rewinding, check your HEAD!`, `Not rewinding to ORIG_HEAD`), leaving the commit on the branch with the rest of the queue gone and nothing to resume. Resume *instead* and the checkpoint follows HEAD — cherry-pick records it when the next pick runs, `git am` on any move to the next patch, `--skip` as much as `--continue` — so the abort after that conflict is allowed and rewinds the whole operation past the commit. Repair by resetting the branch to a commit you name, not by aborting. Measured on two-commit sequences whose first pick or patch conflicted: cherry-pick, commit the resolution, `--abort` → the warning, HEAD on the commit, `.git/sequencer` removed; the same commit, `--continue` to the next conflict, `--abort` → HEAD back at the start. `git am`, commit the resolution, `--skip` (which the `No changes - did you forget to use 'git add'?` message suggests, after `--continue` exits 128 on the now-clean index) → the checkpoint moves from the start up to that commit, and the next `--abort` puts HEAD back at the start with the resolution gone. Where the commit finishes the operation there is nothing left to abort (`no cherry-pick or revert in progress`, `no rebase in progress` after a `--continue` that completes a rebase). `git rebase --abort` rewinds regardless: after a `git commit` inside the rebase it put the branch back where it started. With `rerere` on, an abort keeps the resolution it recorded, and a retry can come back with those lines already in the file: measured, after a rebase was aborted at its second conflict, the next `git rebase` laid the wrong resolution down in place of a fresh conflict with markers. ## Done when The PR is merged, its review findings were fixed or answered on the PR, and the local clone is back on main.

# Before every push

Run these before you open a PR and again before every review-fix push. Fixes cause as many misses as first pushes.

1. **The check script passes.** Run the project's check script (for example `scripts/check.sh`). If the project has none, see `guardrails.md`. In a worktree another agent also edits, stage the files you changed by name before you commit: `git commit -a` takes the other agent's unfinished work too.
2. **Figures come from the shared tool.** Every count, total and ID list is recomputed by the project's tool from the source files, never copied from memory, a summary or an earlier message. Count the population the sentence claims, not a neighbouring one: the listed items, not IDs cited in another item's rationale or explanation. A claim in a pull request body or a commit message counts too: run the search or the count before you write it, not after.
3. **External facts cite a primary source.** Release notes, a changelog, a specification or a filing, with version and date. An open issue, a roadmap or a search snippet is a lead, not a source. A version claim names the first release with full support, not a preview. For anything hosted on GitHub, read it with `gh api` (releases, tags, file contents). Read the primary source itself, not a page about it: on one PR a README's "Version 1 Beta" heading stood in for an ontology file whose maturity annotation said Released. Quote the governing file or filing, and quote the passage whole: the sentence as the source prints it, so its qualifiers come with it.

4. **A change reaches every place it applies.** Search the whole repo for every status, rule, term or figure you change, including text split across lines. When you change a rule, walk every section that depends on it: later pipeline steps, checklists, examples, companion documents, other repos that copy it. When a change adds a member to a set of values (an enum value, a status, a category) or replaces an instruction, also search for the bare old number, the set's other members, and the old instruction's own words, such as the ticket a step used to wait for. A search for the phrases you expect finds only those phrases. If the project's fact tool has a sweep command, run it first: it lists where the wording the branch replaced or deleted still stands. It cannot see the same claim in other words, a one-word change or an addition, so the searches above stay required. Search record header rows and text split across lines too: on one PR a record's header kept an old count that its body had corrected, and on another a count split across two lines escaped a one-line search. Report what you searched in the PR body, under the heading the project requires (for example "Sweep").
5. **Every command the change tells a person to run has been run.** For a runbook, README steps or a guide, run each command, or a harmless version of it (a dry run, a read-only query, a check against a throwaway copy), in the shell the reader uses (zsh on macOS, where `status` is a read-only variable), and check its exit status on the failure path as well as the success path. Say in the PR body which commands ran, and what each printed. *Why:* on one PR, a stores runbook took four review rounds, and most findings were commands nobody had run: a loop that passed silently on failure, a variable zsh refuses, a readiness check that exited 0 when the database never answered, and table names pasted into SQL unquoted.
6. **An independent review runs on the diff, and every finding is fixed or answered.** Use a different model from the one that wrote the change. The table under "Who reviews" in `changing.md` says which reviewers to try, in order, and when one counts as not available. For Kimi, run `herdr-review.sh --kind kimi`, described below. When it names Pi, run `~/.agents/skills/way-of-working/scripts/pi-review.sh --role independent --head <commit> --verify "<claims to verify>"`, with `--since <commit>` for a later round, as a background job, and read its report; that section describes the script. For Codex, run `herdr-review.sh` with no `--kind`. When it names the Cursor agent CLI, use `herdr-review.sh --kind cursor`. The table decides the tool; the host only decides where it runs. `herdr-review.sh` runs when the working agent is inside a Herdr TUI pane (`test -n "${HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID:-}"`, which is what the script checks); inside a Rex pane, where it hands off to `rex-review.sh` ("In Rex" below); or in a terminal of the Herdr app, where it hands off to `hc-review.sh` ("In the Herdr app" below). Outside all three, Kimi and the Cursor agent CLI are not available, and Codex runs through the Codex plugin, described below.

   **Commit the change first, and leave the working tree clean.** A branch review reads committed commits only, so an uncommitted fix is not reviewed at all — an agent that reviews, then edits, then pushes has reviewed the wrong thing. Note the commit you reviewed; if HEAD moves before the push, review again, within the round limit under "Re-review after fixing" below.

   **With Herdr** (the working agent is inside a Herdr pane), spawn a reviewer agent in its own pane — a different kind/model from the writer — and have it run the `ce-code-review` skill, which does a structured multi-agent review (risk-based reviewer selection, parallel reviewers, a cross-model adversarial pass, a validator, and a rendered report). **Reuse the review tab for this repo and reviewer rather than opening a new one for every review.** It is named `review-<repo>-<kind>-<hash>` (the repo's directory name, then the reviewer's kind and a hash of its kind and model) so it is findable:

It acts only for `--kind cursor` and only on the input line, so the marker quoted elsewhere on screen, such as in a diff, sends nothing. On 2026-10-23 herdr read the pane as idle, and the text appeared after the first look.

Zero or several end in exit 1.

      **An earlier review can hold the reviewer's name.** Herdr refuses a name another live agent holds and names the holder's tab, directory and status. When the holder is in this work tree and idle or done, the script closes its tab (`herdr tab close`), prints `closed <tab> (status <status>)` on standard error, and starts once more. The retry always runs: closing the holder restarts the five tries a busy pane gets. When closing another tab fails, the script prints herdr's error and still retries once. When closing the reused review tab fails, the script prints herdr's error, creates no tab, and stops, with `Next:` closing that tab and then running the script again. The holder can be the reused review tab itself, whose pane reads as having no reviewer while herdr still holds the name; the script then closes that tab, creates a fresh one, prints `Review tab: <tab id> (created)`, and starts there. When it is still working or blocked, the script stops without closing it: `Reviewer did not start: another review is running in <tab>; wait for it or close it.`, then a `Next:` line that waits for that review and runs the script again. A holder in another directory is left alone, and the start fails with herdr's error.

      Exit 0 means the report, and only the report, is on standard output. Exit 1 means no report, and every exit 1 ends with two lines: the reason, then `Next: <command>`. After the prompt, the output ends with `Prompt result: <herdr error>` (only if the prompt did not complete), the pane's recent text, then `No report at <path>: <reason>.` and the `Next:` line. Before the prompt, a reviewer that did not start prints herdr's error and the pane, then `Reviewer did not start: <reason>.` and the `Next:` line. Any other early failure (`HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID` unset, a herdr error, no review tab or pane, an unwritable report folder) prints its error on standard error, then `No review: <step> failed; the error is above.` and the `Next:` line. The same two lines end a run that fails or is killed (TERM, INT or HUP, even during the prompt's own wait) once the prompt is on its way. `Next:` then waits for that review and prints its report if the prompt was delivered (it returned, or the reviewer was seen working), and runs the script again if not. Exit 2 means bad arguments. `scripts/test_herdr_review.py` covers each of those cases.

      **Wait for the job's exit status and output before you push or open a pull request.** Launching it returns neither. A non-zero status stops the push. **When it ends without a report**, read the reason, act on it, and run the `Next:` command: `herdr agent wait ... && cat '<path>'` when the review may still be running; `cat '<path>'` when the reviewer's file was still growing; the script again with the same arguments when the reviewer never started or finished without a report; an answer to the reviewer's question (`herdr agent send-keys <pane> <key>`) followed by the wait when it blocked after working, or by the script again when it was blocked before the prompt arrived; and, when several skill reports match, a `cp` of the one you pick after reading them. The review tab shares the working tree, so the reviewer sees the branch you have checked out. For later rounds, run it again with the new commit and say which findings you fixed or answered (see "Re-review after fixing" below). `ce-code-review` is report-only, so apply its findings yourself.

A test rewrites the script mid-run and expects the report.

A question, a trust dialog and an unknown screen all count toward the same two minutes of waiting on a question, and a wait that runs out while one shows ends as waiting on a question.    ```sh
   node "$(ls -d "$HOME"/.claude/plugins/cache/openai-codex/codex/*/scripts/codex-companion.mjs | tail -1)" \

   The plugin takes `--model` but no effort setting, so the review runs at the `model_reasoning_effort` in `~/.codex/config.toml`. Tell it which claims to verify and which documents must stay consistent. Ask it to be adversarial, and to say how the thing under review could still pass while being wrong.

   - **State claims as the change's effects, not as your search.** Name what the change does to the project, in this PR's own terms. For example, a PR that adds an order status and drops a manual approval step should claim "orders gain a status; refunds no longer wait for manual approval", not "every document stating the counts was updated". The reviewer checks what the claim names, so a claim that describes your search confines the review to the places you already looked.
   - **Reproduce every finding before you accept it.** A finding is a claim; run it. A finding accepted on assertion becomes a wrong change.
   - **Fix every place a finding applies, not only the one it names.** Before you fix a finding, name its kind, such as a wording, a rule, or a value crossing a boundary, and search the whole repository for it with the project's search tool. Fix every instance in the same commit, and tell the next round the kind and the search you ran. The review scripts ask the reviewer for the same list, but a reviewer can judge one instance fine and leave it out. One PR took three holds this way, each on a named reference crossing a different validation stage; another took a hold for a gate's scope fixed in two of the three documents that stated it. Name the class, not the instance: a finding about one spelling of a path is about every spelling, and one about one exit path of a script (a signal, a timeout, a hang at exit) is about every exit path. List the class in your reply and test each member, as "Prove a new check fails" below describes. On 2026-10-24 a guard took four further reviews, each finding a rarer spelling of a path, and a review script took six, each finding another exit path.
   - **Fix clear defects; answer judgement calls in the PR body.** Say which is which, so the reviewer can weigh the judgement.
   - **Re-review after fixing, at most two rounds.** A fix can introduce its own defects — a guard tightened in one place is often loosened in another — so run the review again on the fixed diff. A round is one independent review of the branch's head. The limit applies per batch of work:
     - Before the pull request opens, at most two rounds.
     - Each HOLD on the open pull request starts a fresh count of two for the fixes it asks for.

     After the second round of a batch, fix only a finding that would let a wrong result through on input the project will realistically see. This holds for a project's quick checks of later fixes too: a rarer member of a class the change already covers, such as one more encoding of a path, is a follow-up or a judgement call in the PR body, not another fix. List every other finding in the PR body as a follow-up. Push the last fix without another review, and name that unreviewed commit in the PR body. If round two finds the same kind of defect as round one, redesign (next point) instead of patching a third time.
   - **Redesign when tightening a rule starts flagging a *correct* case.** That is the stop signal: a rule tightened to catch one variant of a defect now fails on a case which is right, and no further tightening converges from there — each attempt buys another review round. Change the design instead: what the rule reads, or where in the flow it sits. Say in the PR what design changed and why, then re-check the old variants under the new shape. Narrowing what a check claims is a redesign too: a check that scans text for every way to do a thing loses to the next spelling, while one that pins the exact output of the code that matters (the queries the counts, the hash and the round trip send, captured from a fake session) cannot. Say the narrower claim in the docs that describe the check. Until that redesign lands, variants of one wrong design are not separate bugs to be filed away — three copies of a stale figure are three real defects, and they stay defects. A redesign forced by round two gets one review of its own. That is the only review past the limit.

## Prove a new check fails

When you add a check, break the thing it checks on purpose (change one figure, one status, one record) and confirm the check fails; then restore it. A check that has never failed may pass vacuously.

Clear the interpreter's bytecode cache (`__pycache__` for Python) before each run of a mutation and after restoring it. A mutation the same length as the line it replaces, restored within the same second, can leave a cached copy of the mutant that the next run executes, so a correct tree fails or a broken one passes.

Test the check against the cases it claims, not just the happy path: a guard that hashes names rather than contents, or that follows a symlink, or that reads a file named `-` as standard input, passes every ordinary run and fails none. Enumerate the cases the check claims to catch and make each one fail on purpose.

When the cases form a class of input, such as any character or any spelling a renderer accepts, state the rule on what the renderer produces, not on the source text. Then generate the class in the test: every candidate character at every position. A list of the spellings you thought of is what a reviewer extends one round at a time. One check that a quoted answer renders as plain text took nine review rounds this way, most rounds finding another way to hide markup (indentation, a nested quote, zero-width and control characters). It converged only once the rule read the parser's output. The review that passed it tried every code point at nine positions, a probe the test should have run from the start.

Confirm the test run finished before you read its result, from the runner's own final lines (for example `Ran 95 tests` and `FAILED (failures=20)`), not from a count of its output. A run that never starts or never finishes prints no final result, and a count piped from it still prints a number. One test meant to fail on the unfixed code read as zero failures because the command wrapping it was not installed, so `grep -c` counted the shell's error message. Run without the wrapper, it reported twenty failures.

A test that **reproduces a defect** is held to the same standard: run it against the unfixed code and confirm it fails, for the reason you expect. That is not a rule for every new test. A compatibility or invariant test — a valid input still works, the same answer survives reformatting — passes both versions, and forcing it to fail would delete exactly the coverage `guardrails.md` asks for. But that holds only while the invariant already holds on the unfixed code. When the defect *is* that it does not — reformatting changes the answer — the test must fail there, and it is a defect test like any other.

Watch too for a test that passes for the wrong reason: the input that looks like the bug is not always the one that exercises it.

Take a check that reads backticked spans in documents and treats a digest-shaped one as a pin to verify. It must leave `docker compose up …` alone, where `…` means "and so on", so a test asserts exactly that — and it passed, on a span written the way the docs show it, `! docker compose up …`. The check removes the whitespace inside a span before asking whether the span is a pin at all, and the shell's `!` is no digit or letter, so that span failed on its first character and was never judged. The `!` was doing the work; the ellipsis was never tested. Drop the `!` and the same words join into `dockercomposeup…`, which passes for a digest, and the build fails on a documentation line — the case the test existed to cover. Same words, one character apart, and the assertion held in both runs for reasons that had nothing to do with each other.

So state the input and the assertion, then say why the assertion held. If the reason is not the one you meant to test, the input is wrong.

A test that checks data against a document (a fixture against its specification, a generated file against the table it encodes) compares every fact the document states, not just the identifiers. Comparing names and connections lets a wrong type, value or reference through. Two more steps close the gap:

- **Forbid facts the document does not state.** Compare whole records for exact equality, so an invented value fails.
- **Pin the document text the data was last checked against,** by hash, so any edit to that text fails the test until someone checks the data again. A parser reads only the facts it was written for and cannot notice an edit to the rest; the pin can.

All six hold, and the PR body says that they ran and what the review found.

# Ontology reuse baseline — Enterprise Context Engineering

**Status:** Proposed (survey result, 2026-11-08; not a recorded decision)
**Purpose:** Name the publicly available ontologies ECE imports or borrows patterns from when the semantic layer is constructed, so the import set is decided once instead of rediscovered per artifact.
**Related:** [Shared Technical Foundation](shared-technical-foundation.md) section 11 fixes the *formats* (SKOS, RDF-star, SHACL, SSSOM); this document picks the *public vocabularies* underneath those formats. Charter section 7, item 3 leaves the EPM Downstream Oil and Gas Ontology import as an open decision; the oil-and-gas section below feeds that decision.

Method: a web survey on 2026-11-08 of candidate ontologies across ten coverage areas (upper structure, provenance, time, data products and units, industrial/OT, events, organization, decisions, downstream oil and gas, documents). Licenses and activity dates were read from the GitHub API, W3C TR pages and the ETSI portal on that date, not from search snippets, except where marked. Re-verify each entry before an actual import; activity dates below say "pushed" as of 2026-11-08.

## 1. Adopt (core import set)

| Ontology | ECE layer | License | Maturity | Use in ECE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [PROV-O](https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-o/) (W3C TR, verified) | provenance, governance | W3C license | W3C Recommendation, 2013 | Claim-level provenance backbone: entities, activities, agents, derivation. |
| [OWL-Time](https://www.w3.org/TR/owl-time/) (W3C TR, verified) | provenance, semantic | W3C license | W3C Recommendation, 2017 | Authoring time, decision time, effective-period semantics in the graph. |
| [DCAT 3](https://www.w3.org/TR/vocab-dcat-3/) (W3C TR, verified) | semantic, governance | W3C license | W3C Recommendation, 2024 | Release catalogs: datasets, distributions, manifests. |
| [SKOS](https://www.w3.org/TR/skos-reference/) | semantic | W3C license | W3C Recommendation, 2009 | Taxonomy and shared vocabulary; already fixed by the format baseline. |
| [QUDT](https://github.com/qudt/qudt-public-repo) | semantic | CC-BY-4.0 (GitHub API) | actively maintained (pushed 2026-11-06) | Units, quantities and dimensions for KPIs and engineer data; published in an **all-in-one SHACL** build, so it validates at import time. |
| [SSN/SOSA](https://www.w3.org/TR/vocab-ssn/) (W3C TR, verified) | semantic, provenance | W3C license | W3C Recommendation, 2017 | Sensors and observations: historian windows, alarms, lab data. |
| [ORG](https://www.w3.org/TR/vocab-org/) (W3C TR, verified) | semantic | W3C license | W3C Recommendation, 2014 | Organizations, roles, reporting structures. |
| [ODRL 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/odrl-vocab/) (W3C TR, verified) | governance | W3C license | W3C Recommendation, 2018 | Source-classification and access policies on artifacts. |

These eight are light, standard, and license-clean. They carry infrastructure meaning only; none of them speaks about KPIs, decisions, evidence or epistemic status, which is where ECE's own vocabulary sits.

## 2. Adopt with caveats

| Ontology | Use in ECE | Caveat |
|---|---|---|
| [DPROD](https://github.com/ekgf/dprod) (EKGF/OMG workgroup, since 2024) | RDF/OWL data-product vocabulary for release namespace and contract metadata | Actively maintained (pushed 2026-11-08), but the GitHub license reads `NOASSERTION`. Pin the license from the workgroup's primary source before importing. |
| [IOF Core](https://spec.industrialontologies.org/) (OAGi) | Manufacturing-grade core: measurement, process, resource concepts | MIT license per the OAGi/IOF portal. The GitHub mirror `iofoundry/Core` is archived (read-only since 2022-10); the spec portal is canonical. |
| [BFO](https://github.com/BFO-ontology/BFO) | Top level if ECE follows the IOF route | CC-BY-4.0 (GitHub API), last pushed 2024-01. Choose one upper ontology: BFO (when IOF concepts are wanted) or GIST below — do not import both. |
| [GIST](https://github.com/semanticarts/gist) (Semantic Arts) | Simpler enterprise upper ontology alternative to BFO | CC-BY-4.0 (GitHub API), very active (pushed 2026-11-03). Lighter than BFO; weaker when IOF's manufacturing detail is wanted. |
| [SAREF suite](https://saref.etsi.org/) (ETSI) | Systems, industry and manufacturing extensions behind SAREF4INMA and SAREF4SYST | ETSI publishes the suite free and versioned. `saref.etsi.org/saref4industry/` returned 404 during the survey; confirm the intended extension page before use. |
| [EPCIS 2.0 + CBV](https://www.gs1.org/standards/epcis) (GS1) | Event vocabulary with what/when/where/why/how | Standard is freely available; check whether importing the RDF vocabulary or restating its event shapes is the better fit, since EPCIS is supply-chain oriented. |
| [PREMIS OWL](https://www.loc.gov/standards/premis/ontology/) (Library of Congress) | Documents and records as evidence objects: objects, events, agents | Verified on the LoC page; heavier than PROV-O alone. Borrow its document/record shapes rather than importing wholesale. |

## 3. Borrow patterns only

| Candidate | Why not a dependency |
|---|---|
| [Decision Ontology (DO)](https://github.com/nicholascar/do-ont) | Directly on target for decisions, but last pushed 2018-04 and small (CC-BY-4.0 per GitHub API). Reuse its class shapes (decision, decision-making, options, rationale) as the starting pattern; keep the implementation in ECE's own namespace, where PROV-O can anchor agents and activities. |
| [W3C Decision Incubator model](https://www.w3.org/2005/Incubator/decision/XGR-decision-20120417/Sample_Decision_Ontology.html) (2012) | Superseded; DO above is its continuation. Reference only. |

## 4. Rejected or marginal

| Candidate | Reason |
|---|---|
| [OM (Ontology of units of Measure)](http://www.ontology-of-units-of-measure.org/resource/om-2) | Host unreachable during the survey; QUDT covers the need with better tooling. |
| [ODPS](https://opendataproducts.org/) / [Data Product Specification](https://github.com/agile-lab-dev/Data-Product-Specification) | YAML/JSON specifications, not vocabularies. DPROD is the RDF option for data products. |
| [Accenture OSDU-Ontology](https://github.com/Accenture/OSDU-Ontology) | Apache-2.0, pushed 2024-12, but upstream/subsurface-biased and a single-vendor artifact (38 stars). Reference for source-system alignment, not an import. |
| [OpenEnergy Ontology](https://github.com/OpenEnergyPlatform/ontology) | CC0 and very active, but energy-policy focused; tangential to downstream refining. |
| FaBiO / BIBO | Scholarly-bibliographic focus; PREMIS plus PROV-O cover ECE's document case. |
| DOLCE/UFO/DOL, CCO | Evidence too thin during the survey: no well-maintained release artifact surfaced that could be verified directly. Re-examine only if BFO/GIST both disappoint. |

## 5. Keep bespoke

No maintained public ontology surfaced for these ECE needs; each is planned as ECE's own vocabulary:

- **Epistemic status** — direct evidence, inference, contradiction, unknown. A 2025 survey of provenance/assertion/evidence ontologies exists, and nothing adopted-and-maintained surfaced from it.
- **The two axes** — source/data classification and epistemic status tracked separately. This separation is ECE's own design, not a known vocabulary.
- **KPI governance** — owner, calculation meaning, KPI lineage. QUDT and DCAT give units and catalog entries; they do not speak to KPI stewardship.
- **Claim locators** — pinpointing a claim inside a source artifact (slide, page, historian window, query). PROV-O needs ECE-specific refinements here; the W3C Web Annotation model is an unverified follow-up candidate for exactly this shape.
- **Downstream refining vocabulary** — processes, value streams, products, units of the worked example. See section 6.

## 6. Oil and gas: public standards versus the EPM ontology

The public downstream picture is thin, and this is the strongest input for charter section 7, item 3. The process-asset vocabulary is genuinely public: ISO 15926 is an ISO standard, but its ontology artifacts are available free from the [PCA reference data services](https://rds.posccaesar.org/services/downloads/) in Turtle, RDF-XML and JSON-LD, and ISO 15926-14 reconciles 15926 with W3C recommendations. OSDU follows subsurface definitions, and its RDF coverage is a small single-vendor bridge. Neither gives downstream refining, product, or market vocabulary. The working recommendation stands: **import the EPM Downstream Oil and Gas Ontology for domain truth; borrow ISO 15926/PCA vocabulary for asset and equipment structure; treat OSDU as a source-system alignment reference rather than an import.** That decision stays open until recorded under the charter's process.

## 7. Runtime note: RDF inside Neo4j

If the graph is served from Neo4j, [neosemantics (n10s)](https://github.com/neo4j-labs/neosemantics) imports RDF (Apache-2.0, pushed 2026-11-06) and runs SHACL validation in-graph. This is the bridge between the imported vocabularies above and the operational context graph; it is infrastructure, not an ontology.

# Code review: `docs/ontology-reuse-baseline` vs `main`

**Verdict: Not ready**  
**Scope:** merge-base `42ae9ac0e564e3eff7610cd8e975b6cc6f9c92a4`; two changed documentation files; 71 additions and 1 deletion.  
**Mode:** report only. No findings were applied.

## Findings

### #1 — P1 — Incomplete license guidance omits QUDT's third-party UCUM terms

- **Defect kind:** license/compliance omission.
- **Primary location:** `docs/architecture/ontology-reuse-baseline.md:17`.
- **Every repository occurrence:**
  - `docs/architecture/ontology-reuse-baseline.md:17` reduces the QUDT entry to `CC-BY-4.0 (GitHub API)`.
  - `docs/architecture/ontology-reuse-baseline.md:22` then calls the entire eight-item core set `license-clean` without qualifying the separate UCUM terms.
  - No occurrences outside the diff were found by the repository-wide QUDT/UCUM/license search.
- **First evidence:** `docs/architecture/ontology-reuse-baseline.md:17 -- | [QUDT](https://github.com/qudt/qudt-public-repo) | semantic | CC-BY-4.0 (GitHub API) | actively maintained (pushed 2026-11-06) | Units, quantities and dimensions for KPIs and engineer data; published in an **all-in-one SHACL** build, so it validates at import time. |`
- **Why it matters:** an importer can record only CC BY 4.0 and miss the separate obligations attached to UCUM codes and archived UCUM resources in QUDT distributions. The GitHub API result is correct for the repository's root license, but it is not a complete inventory of third-party material.
- **Evidence:** QUDT's primary [licensing document](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/qudt/qudt-public-repo/main/LICENSING.md) states that QUDT sources and distributions are CC BY 4.0, while UCUM codes and archived UCUM resources are third-party material under the UCUM license: “Your use of it is also subject to the UCUM license terms.”
- **How this could pass review while still being wrong:** the documented SPDX value exactly matches the GitHub API, so a metadata-only check passes. That check never reads QUDT's `LICENSING.md` and therefore cannot detect the omitted third-party terms.
- **Suggested fix:** retain CC BY 4.0 for QUDT, add the UCUM license for included UCUM material with a link to `LICENSING.md`, and qualify the blanket `license-clean` sentence accordingly.
- **Route / confidence:** `gated_auto`, `downstream-resolver`; confidence 75; `requires_verification: true`; `pre_existing: false`.
- **Reviewers:** correctness and the independent local adversarial reviewer. Agreement is same-family and was not used to promote confidence.

### #2 — P2 — QUDT's SHACL artifact is incorrectly said to validate at import time

- **Defect kind:** false technical/capability claim.
- **Primary location:** `docs/architecture/ontology-reuse-baseline.md:17`.
- **Every repository occurrence:** only `docs/architecture/ontology-reuse-baseline.md:17` contains this import-time QUDT validation claim. Other SHACL references describe validation as an explicit write-time or in-graph operation, not as a consequence of importing QUDT. No occurrence outside the diff was found.
- **First evidence:** `docs/architecture/ontology-reuse-baseline.md:17 -- | [QUDT](https://github.com/qudt/qudt-public-repo) | semantic | CC-BY-4.0 (GitHub API) | actively maintained (pushed 2026-11-06) | Units, quantities and dimensions for KPIs and engineer data; published in an **all-in-one SHACL** build, so it validates at import time. |`
- **Why it matters:** a reader can expect loading QUDT's all-in-one SHACL graph to validate QUDT or ECE KPI data automatically. Shipping a SHACL distribution does not itself execute a SHACL validator, and QUDT's user rules do not establish ECE instance-data conformance.
- **Evidence:** QUDT's [README](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/qudt/qudt-public-repo/main/README.md) does ship `QUDT-all-in-one-SHACL.ttl`, so that part of the row is correct. Its validation section says the user rules check references to deprecated instances or properties; contributor validation uses a larger rule set through individual graphs. The repository's own `docs/architecture/shared-technical-foundation.md:115` separately assigns SHACL to write-time validation.
- **How this could pass review while still being wrong:** a reviewer can confirm that the all-in-one SHACL filename exists and that SHACL is a validation technology, then accept the causal phrase without checking what the bundled rules validate or when a validator runs.
- **Suggested fix:** keep the all-in-one SHACL distribution claim, but replace `so it validates at import time` with the actual deprecated-reference checks and state that ECE must run a validator explicitly and author its own KPI shapes.
- **Route / confidence:** `gated_auto`, `downstream-resolver`; confidence 75; `requires_verification: true`; `pre_existing: false`.
- **Reviewers:** correctness and the independent local adversarial reviewer; no confidence promotion.

### #3 — P2 — CCO is rejected for lack of artifacts that publicly exist

- **Defect kind:** factually incorrect survey/rejection rationale.
- **Primary location:** `docs/architecture/ontology-reuse-baseline.md:52`.
- **Every repository occurrence:** only `docs/architecture/ontology-reuse-baseline.md:52` mentions CCO, Common Core Ontologies, or this rejection rationale. No occurrence outside the diff was found.
- **First evidence:** `docs/architecture/ontology-reuse-baseline.md:52 -- | DOLCE/UFO/DOL, CCO | Evidence too thin during the survey: no well-maintained release artifact surfaced that could be verified directly. Re-examine only if BFO/GIST both disappoint. |`
- **Why it matters:** the survey removes CCO from consideration for an incorrect availability reason, preventing readers from assessing its actual fit, license, or modernization risks.
- **Evidence:** the canonical [CommonCoreOntologies repository](https://api.github.com/repos/CommonCoreOntology/CommonCoreOntologies) says it holds the current released suite, is not archived, reports `pushed_at` `2026-10-02T16:16:49Z`, and reports BSD-3-Clause. Its [v2.2 release](https://github.com/CommonCoreOntology/CommonCoreOntologies/releases/latest), published 2026-08-14, provides `CommonCoreOntologiesMerged-2.2.ttl`, `CCO-2.2-modules.zip`, `ModalRelationOntology-2.2.ttl`, and checksums. The [README](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CommonCoreOntology/CommonCoreOntologies/develop/README.md) documents planned 3.0/4.0 structural changes, which could support a stability caveat but not an absence-of-artifact claim.
- **How this could pass review while still being wrong:** CCO is grouped with three unrelated candidates and has no link in the row, so a reviewer can accept a broad “evidence too thin” judgment without inspecting the canonical CCO repository. The requested checks cover other ontologies and never exercise this negative claim.
- **Suggested fix:** split CCO from DOLCE/UFO/DOL, cite its canonical repository and release artifacts, and assess fitness or modernization stability explicitly rather than claiming that no maintained release artifact could be verified.
- **Route / confidence:** `gated_auto`, `downstream-resolver`; confidence 75; `requires_verification: true`; `pre_existing: false`.
- **Reviewers:** correctness and the independent local adversarial reviewer; no confidence promotion.

### #4 — P2 — Prescriptive import wording obscures the proposal-only status

- **Defect kind:** status/intent contradiction at the point of use.
- **Primary location:** `docs/architecture/shared-technical-foundation.md:120`.
- **Every repository occurrence of this baseline's import-set wording:**
  - `docs/architecture/ontology-reuse-baseline.md:4` says ECE `imports` these ontologies and the set `is decided once`.
  - `docs/architecture/ontology-reuse-baseline.md:5` says the document `picks` the public vocabularies.
  - `docs/architecture/ontology-reuse-baseline.md:9` labels the core set `Adopt`.
  - `docs/architecture/ontology-reuse-baseline.md:24` labels the next set `Adopt with caveats`.
  - `docs/architecture/shared-technical-foundation.md:120` calls them `The concrete public ontologies to import`.
  - No additional occurrence of this specific baseline or its import-set wording exists outside the diff. Other proposed EPM-import statements are separate pre-existing architecture content, not occurrences of this new public-ontology baseline.
- **First evidence:** `docs/architecture/shared-technical-foundation.md:120 -- Section 2's stack provides the server layer for this work: Jena/Fuseki with SHACL and SPARQL. The concrete public ontologies to import under these formats are named in the [ontology reuse baseline](ontology-reuse-baseline.md). Three lightweight libraries complete it, entering per section 3 only when a pipeline requirement justifies them: pySHACL for standalone SHACL validation in generation and test pipelines, Skosify to convert RDFS/OWL vocabularies to SKOS, and RDFLib for RDF processing in Python.`
- **Why it matters:** a maintainer or generator following the foundation can treat surveyed candidates as authorized dependencies even though the baseline's header says `Proposed` and `not a recorded decision`. The link is the point of use, and it drops the candidate qualification.
- **Evidence:** `docs/architecture/ontology-reuse-baseline.md:3` is explicitly proposal-only, while the locations above use completed-selection language. `docs/charter.md:68-74` requires proposal, review, and explicit approval rather than implied approval.
- **How this could pass review while still being wrong:** a status check sees `Status: Proposed` in both documents and stops. It does not evaluate whether the linked architecture and section headings tell a downstream reader to adopt the set anyway.
- **Suggested fix:** use `candidate public ontologies proposed for import` in the foundation, change `picks` to `proposes`, rename the adoption headings as proposed sets, and make the Purpose say the set is decided only after the required review.
- **Route / confidence:** `gated_auto`, `downstream-resolver`; confidence 75; `requires_verification: true`; `pre_existing: false`.
- **Reviewers:** correctness and the independent local adversarial reviewer; no confidence promotion.

These requested checks match the document; they are not findings.

1. **DPROD:** the [GitHub API](https://api.github.com/repos/ekgf/dprod) reports `license.spdx_id: NOASSERTION` and `pushed_at: 2026-11-08T00:41:50Z`.

Findings #1 and #2 concern the conclusions drawn from those correct facts, not the facts themselves.
3. **IOF Core:** the [repository API](https://api.github.com/repos/iofoundry/Core) reports `archived: true` and MIT; the [GitHub page](https://github.com/iofoundry/Core/blob/main/Core.rdf) states that it was archived on 2022-10-20. The [specification portal](https://spec.industrialontologies.org/) presents current IOF releases generated from `iofoundry/ontology`, supporting it as the canonical source rather than the archived `iofoundry/Core` mirror. The portal describes distribution under MIT.
4. **W3C Recommendation years:** all seven years are correct: [PROV-O, 2013-04-30](https://www.w3.org/TR/2013/REC-prov-o-20130430/); [OWL-Time, 2017-10-19](https://www.w3.org/TR/2017/REC-owl-time-20171019/); [DCAT 3, 2024-08-22](https://www.w3.org/TR/2024/REC-vocab-dcat-3-20240822/); [ORG, 2014-01-16](https://www.w3.org/TR/2014/REC-vocab-org-20140116/); [ODRL 2.2, 2018-02-15](https://www.w3.org/TR/2018/REC-odrl-vocab-20180215/); [SSN/SOSA, 2017-10-19](https://www.w3.org/TR/2017/REC-vocab-ssn-20171019/); and [SKOS, 2009-08-18](https://www.w3.org/TR/2009/REC-skos-reference-20090818/).
5. **SAREF:** `https://saref.etsi.org/saref4industry/` returned HTTP 404 during this review, matching the document.
6. **Decision Ontology:** the [GitHub API](https://api.github.com/repos/nicholascar/do-ont) reports `CC-BY-4.0` and `pushed_at: 2018-04-07T03:27:33Z`.
7. **Relative links and status:** the new document's relative link to `shared-technical-foundation.md` resolves, as does the new reverse link. `python3 scripts/check_doc_links.py` passed: `OK: 55 relative doc links resolve.` The only status header claimed by the new document is `Proposed`; no Accepted or Approved status was found. Finding #4 records the separate problem created by prescriptive wording despite that header.

## Actionable findings

All four retained findings are actionable as `gated_auto` / `downstream-resolver`: #1, #2, #3, and #4. This is a routing summary only; no fix was applied.

## Coverage and limits

- Focused review: parent correctness review plus one completed independent local adversarial reviewer. The cross-model pass was not run because this host's serving family could not be attested. No validator ran on this focused path.
- Repository-wide searches covered every retained defect's terms and synonyms, including content outside the diff. Additional occurrences are listed explicitly above; there are no unlisted occurrences of the specific retained claims.
- No `AGENTS.md`, `REVIEW_STANDARDS.md`, `CODING_STANDARDS.md`, or `CLAUDE.md` exists in this checkout, so no repository standards file supplied additional criteria. Declared Compound Packs were not present or applied.
- No plan was discovered, so requirements completeness was not assessed. Learnings, agent-native gaps, and deployment notes were not assessed.
- `scripts/check_doc_links.py` validates relative filesystem links only. External facts were checked manually against primary sources during this review; there is no repeatable source snapshot or external-claim test that would make the date-sensitive survey reproducible later.
- Residual risk: repository metadata and web pages are point-in-time observations. The document already tells readers to re-verify before an actual import.

## 1. Core import set

### 1a. Already named by the section 11 baseline

These four appear in section 11's standards table today; this document re-proposes them as concrete imports and adds license and activity verification (all checked 2026-11-08):

| Ontology | ECE layer | License | Maturity | Use in ECE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [SKOS](https://www.w3.org/TR/skos-reference/) | semantic | W3C license | W3C Recommendation, 2009 | Taxonomy and shared vocabulary; section 11 already names it (plus SKOS-XL). |
| [PROV-O](https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-o/) (W3C TR, verified) | provenance, governance | W3C license | W3C Recommendation, 2013 | Claim-level provenance backbone: entities, activities, agents, derivation; section 11 already names it for `semantic/ontology/`. |
| [OWL-Time](https://www.w3.org/TR/owl-time/) (W3C TR, verified) | provenance, semantic | W3C license | W3C Recommendation, 2017 | Authoring time, decision time, effective-period semantics in the graph; section 11 already names it beside PROV-O. |
| [DCAT 3](https://www.w3.org/TR/vocab-dcat-3/) (W3C TR, verified) | semantic, governance | W3C license | W3C Recommendation, 2024 | Release catalogs: datasets, distributions, manifests; section 11 already names it (with DCMI Terms) for release manifests. |
| [DCMI Terms](https://www.dublincore.org/specifications/dublin-core/dcmi-terms/) | semantic, governance | DCMI license | DCMI maintained | Dublin Core Terms for artifact metadata alongside DCAT; section 11 already names it next to DCAT. |

### 1b. Newly proposed here

Candidates until this proposal is approved:

| Ontology | ECE layer | License | Maturity | Use in ECE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [QUDT](https://github.com/qudt/qudt-public-repo) | semantic | CC-BY-4.0, plus a third-party UCUM license on the bundled UCUM codes ([LICENSING.md](https://github.com/qudt/qudt-public-repo/blob/main/LICENSING.md)) (GitHub API) | actively maintained (pushed 2026-11-06) | Units, quantities and dimensions for KPIs and engineer data. Published as an all-in-one SHACL distribution, but its user-level rules only check for deprecated instances and properties: ECE must run a SHACL validator explicitly and author its own KPI shapes on top. |
| [SSN/SOSA](https://www.w3.org/TR/vocab-ssn/) (W3C TR, verified) | semantic, provenance | W3C license | W3C Recommendation, 2017 | Sensors and observations: historian windows, alarms, lab data. |
| [ORG](https://www.w3.org/TR/vocab-org/) (W3C TR, verified) | semantic | W3C license | W3C Recommendation, 2014 | Organizations, roles, reporting structures. |
| [ODRL 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/odrl-vocab/) (W3C TR, verified) | governance | W3C license | W3C Recommendation, 2018 | Source-classification and access policies on artifacts. |

Section 11's four named vocabularies carry its existing status already; the four newly proposed candidates are not dependencies until this proposal is approved. All of them are light, standard, and license-clean apart from QUDT's third-party UCUM terms, noted above, and none of them speaks about KPIs, decisions, evidence or epistemic status, which is where ECE's own vocabulary sits.

The requested HOLD fix is therefore internally inconsistent even though the required closing sentences are present.

**How this could pass review while still being wrong:** A checklist that verifies only the new Related line, the 1a/1b headings, the closing line, and the foundation pointer will pass. It will not notice that the unchanged Purpose paragraph still applies the old blanket gate to every set.
